documents.abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption grows, improving EV charging management depends on accurate forecasts of charging demand and station occupancy, along with effective route guidance and dynamic charging-selection policies. Yet many existing approaches address only one component and do not provide an end-to-end pipeline that handles multiple goals. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a sequential, multi-stage framework that predicts EV charging volume and occupancy under dynamic conditions while simultaneously optimising objectives such as routing, congestion, and cost. For forecasting, the framework uses an LSTM–Transformer model to learn both local and global dependencies and to deliver multi-horizon predictions. For optimisation, it applies reinforcement learning with proximal policy optimisation (RL-PPO), improving decisions by utilising a predicted feature map. In addition, the forecasting signals and agent outputs are leveraged to produce interpretable, LLM-based explanations, helping users to better understand the model’s predictions. The framework is evaluated on diverse datasets, including urban networks from two public benchmarks (UrbanEV and Multi-Faceted) and custom data from the Al Jouf region in Saudi Arabia. The results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness, achieving minimum RMSE values of 0.3244, 0.9339, and 0.15, with predictions closely matching the observed signals. In the optimisation stage, the proposed RL-PPO method achieves the best performance across all three datasets in terms of distance (km), congestion, and waiting time, resulting in higher customer satisfaction and a stronger trade-off than competing methods. Overall, the study delivers accurate forecasting, optimised decision support, and human-readable explanations, enabling an intelligent EV charging system.

The increasing use of various types of probabilistic AI technologies in decision-making roles limits the usefulness of traditional business analysis and design (B&A) methods for documenting non-AI decision-makers and other aspects of probabilistic AI systems‚ including human backup decision-making roles․ Traditional UML and other business analysis tools support only binary decision outcomes and offer few tools for documenting the shared decision-making responsibilities of AI and human decision makers․ This paper proposes an AI-Socio B&A method that integrates traditional business analysis methods with three new tools:(1) a Confidence-Based Delegation Matrix offering three levels of AI decision-making authority (automatic decision making when confidence exceeds 80%‚ assisted decision making when confidence is between 50% and 80%‚ and human backup decision making when confidence is below 50%); (2) an amended use case format that offers additional documentation of confidence levels and bias-prevention techniques along with other information; (3) a process for obtaining and using feedback from human decision makers to improve the AI system․ A case study of an AI-Powered Job Applicant Screening and Short-listing System‚ including documentation of an extended use case (UC-02)‚ actors matrix‚ two design diagrams‚ and comparison with traditional B&A and UML documentation on five design and safety metrics‚ illustrates use of the new AI-Socio B&A method․ Advantages of AI-Socio B&A include reduced automation bias and inclusion of anonymization as a requirement and other tools to share work between human and AI decision makers․

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence technology is gradually being integrated into mental health service contexts and is increasingly discussed as a potential supplementary resource to university mental health support systems. However, AI-based mental health services involve sensitive factors such as emotional expression, personal privacy, and relational interaction. Therefore, college students’ willingness to accept AI-based mental health services and the potential factors associated with such acceptance remain unclear. Based on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, this study introduces six factors—Accessibility (ACC), Privacy Concern (PC), Perceived Anthropomorphism (PA), Perceived Empathy (EMP), Trust (TRU), and Perceived Usefulness (PU)—to systematically examine their relationships with university students’ Behavioral Intention (BI) to use AI-based mental health services. A total of 375 volunteers participated in the current study and completed relevant questionnaires. Structural equation modeling was employed for data analysis. The results indicate that accessibility, perceived usefulness, and trust are all significantly and positively associated with behavioral intention. Perceived empathy is significantly and positively associated with trust, whereas privacy concern is significantly and negatively associated with both trust and behavioral intention. The analysis of indirect effects shows that there is a significant sequential indirect association between perceived anthropomorphism and behavioral intention through perceived empathy, trust, and perceived usefulness. In addition, a significant negative indirect association between privacy concern and behavioral intention through trust was observed. The findings indicate that, in the highly sensitive context of mental health services, college students’ intention to use AI-based mental health services is associated with a combination of accessibility, perceived usefulness, emotional interaction experience, privacy-related evaluations, and trust.

The extensive usage of AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini, has led to a complete transformation of the ways young people acquire information, conduct their academic assignments, and perform technical tasks. However, with the rise in popularity of these platforms, worries emerge regarding the protection of users' information while exchanging it on these sites. The purpose of this study is to identify the degree of awareness regarding the problem of data privacy among young people who use AI chatbots in the state of Maharashtra. The descriptive approach was applied in the research process, and primary data were collected through the use of Google Forms surveys. The sample consisted of 151 respondents aged 15-29 who utilized AI chatbots and exchanged personal information, privacy measures, risks, knowledge about the storage and training of the model, and data protection laws. Some of the AI systems that were in common usage include ChatGPT and Google Gemini, while the type of information that was in widespread sharing included academic information. However, there is one other important observation on the lack of privacy settings, the lack of awareness of storing conversations, and also the limited self-reported awareness of the Indian Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 or similar data laws. The findings of this research suggest the need for proper digital privacy education, clear privacy information in different languages, proper data sharing, and awareness programs.

documents.abstract: This study investigated the dynamics of student engagement within active learning environments, specifically analyzing the relationships between students' attitudes and their behavioral, emotional, and cognitive involvement. Utilizing quantitative research, particularly a descriptive-correlational research design, this study identified the levels of student engagement and evaluated its relationship with their attitude in active learning activities. Through complete enumeration sampling, 44 teacher education students were identified, and their responses were analyzed through weighted means and the Pearson (r) product-moment correlation coefficient. Findings revealed that students are "Highly Engaged" across all measured dimensions, with Grand Means for Behavioral (M=3.78), Emotional (M=3.84), and Cognitive Engagement (M=3.77) reflecting substantial student investment. Statistical analysis confirmed significant positive correlations (p < 0.001) between students' attitudes—notably their Willingness to Participate and Perceived Usefulness—and their engagement levels. Specifically, the strong correlation between Willingness to Participate and Cognitive Engagement (r = 0.79) suggested that students’ internal readiness is closely associated with metacognitive processing and deep learning. The study concluded that engagement may be understood as a dynamic and reciprocal system in which positive attitudes are strongly linked to meaningful learning processes. The practical implications suggest that educators should prioritize confidence-building, low-stakes activities, and structured peer-facilitation roles to help create a supportive classroom community. By fostering a positive “Attitude Filter,” instructors may enhance conditions that support student retention and academic mastery.

The introduction of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and external tools has substantially improved the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on general and reasoning tasks. However, existing fast-slow reasoning paradigms mainly regulate textual reasoning length, while visual computation introduced by external tools or visual tokens is often treated as an auxiliary component. This separation prevents MLLMs from jointly optimizing visual perception and textual reasoning. To address this issue, we propose L2T (adaptive Look, flexible Thought), a unified reasoning framework that jointly optimizes the form and depth of computation. L2T first discretizes tool-produced visual states into visual tokens, bringing visual perception and textual reasoning into a shared autoregressive space. Based on this unified representation, L2T introduces a modality-aware routing reward to select appropriate reasoning modes and a difficulty-aware fast-slow strategy to adapt reasoning depth according to task complexity. Experiments on general perception and reasoning-intensive tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of L2T. Compared with explicit tool-calling approaches, L2T maintains competitive performance while achieving 1.7--3.6 times higher throughput.

Hou-Hsun Liao,1– 3 Yu-Sheng Liu,1 Ying-To Hsu,4 Ming-Hsien Yeh,1 Szu-Chin Li,5,6 Tzung-Yi Tsai7,81Department of Chinese Medicine, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan; 2Department of Biochemical Science and Technology, College of Life Sciences, National Chiayi University, Chiayi City, Taiwan; 3Master Program in Integrated Medicine and Pharmacy Science, College of Life Sciences, National Chiayi University, Chiayi City, Taiwan; 4Division of Allergy, Immunology and Rheumatology, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan; 5School of Medicine, Tzu Chi University, Hualien, Taiwan; 6Division of Hematology and Oncology, Department of Internal Medicine, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan; 7Department of Environmental and Occupational Health, College of Medicine, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan; 8Department of Medical Research, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, TaiwanCorrespondence: Szu-Chin Li; Tzung-Yi Tsai, Email lisrau@gmail.com; dm732024@tzuchi.com.twBackground: Systemic chemotherapy increases the risk of thrombocytopenia in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which may lead to risk of bleeding and treatment interruption. Accumulating evidence indicates that traditional Chinese medicinal herbs (TCMH) may accelerate symptom relief. We hypothesized that integrating TCMH alongside standard treatment may decrease the risk of chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (CIT) in patients with AML.Aim: To compare the likelihood of CIT among patients with AML who received adjunctive TCMH plus standard treatment and those who received standard treatment alone.Methods: This nested case–control study analyzed individuals aged 20 and older who were newly diagnosed with AML, had no pre-existing CIT, and were identified from the Taiwan National Health Insurance Research Database between 2002 and 2010. Five controls were then randomly matched to each CIT case from the remaining eligible cohort. All participants were followed until December 31, 2013. Conditional logistic regression was used to assess the association between TCMH use and risk of developing CIT.Results: TCMH was prescribed in 5.5% of cases and 20.6% of controls. Combining TCMH treatment with standard therapy substantially reduced risk of CIT (OR= 0.21; 95% CI:0.11– 0.39). The inverse association between adjunctive TCMH use and CIT was strongest among patients who received TCMH for more than 180 days. Age and gender did not influence the association between TCMH use and the risk of CIT.Conclusion: The current research emphasized the importance of framing a collaborative healthcare model for AML persons, especially involvement of TCMH, to effectively manage the poor complications that arise from cancer therapy.Keywords: acute myeloid leukemia, chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, traditional Chinese medicinal herbs, nested case–control study, chemotherapy

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to make water management more intuitive through natural language interfaces. However, the generalised training of these models limits their effectiveness at domain-specific tasks such as stormwater modelling, particularly when nuanced answers require executing and modifying water models. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) addresses this challenge by providing a standardised interface for LLMs to interact with external tools while enforcing guardrails for quality control. Building on this protocol, we introduce SWMM-MCP, a cross-platform, model agnostic framework that enables conversational interaction with the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s Stormwater Management Model (EPA SWMM). SWMM-MCP leverages the swmm_api and PySWMM libraries through an MCP server built with FAST-MCP, allowing users to configure, modify, and evaluate SWMM models via natural language. We demonstrate SWMM-MCP using a benchmark task and prompt-response evaluations comparing performance using eight different base LLMs. For the benchmark SWMM task, all base LLMs completed the tasks, but at varying levels of computational efficiency and detailed responses. For the prompt-response evaluations, the LLMs exhibited distinct personalities. Results highlight that even within a structured MCP framework, LLM selection significantly affects task efficiency and domain specific prompting remains important for optimal performance.

Agent-to-agent protocols allow LLM agents to discover peers, exchange results, and coordinate tool use. A locally successful protocol attack, however, may be rejected by a later agent or propagated into a consequential task decision. Measuring local exploitability alone leaves this difference unresolved and provides limited evidence about which participant caused the final outcome. We present Agent-Canary-Mas, an end-to-end evaluation system that follows protocol risk through long-horizon multi-agent tasks. It covers five risk classes and 13 subclasses across A2A, ANP, and BCS, with 975 matched malicious--benign task pairs in five business domains. A shared OpenClaw framework runs autonomous, tool-using agents under different underlying models while preserving the task and execution setup. Matched runs separate local protocol success from downstream consequences; retained evidence connects participant selection, message consumption, tool activity, and task-state changes. We further evaluate a protocol-context Guard that checks an object's authority at consequential handoffs. Across three model conditions, local attack success is frequently at or above 90%, while consequence conversion ranges from 7.1\% to 100.0\%. Cross-agent evidence raises macro-averaged Audit-F1 from 29.7% to 95.5%. On Finance tasks, the Guard lowers average ASR from 86.1% to 53.8% and PTCR from 65.5% to 31.2%, with a measurable completion tradeoff. These results show that protocol risk depends on how agents use exchanged objects throughout the task, and that evaluating this path supports more informative risk assessment, attribution, and defense.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed smart surveillance systems, significantly leveraging technologies such as deep learning, computer vision, and adaptive monitoring. Driven by the need for real‐time object detection, behavioral analysis, and automated alerting, AI‐powered surveillance is increasingly vital for enhancing public safety, operational efficiency, and decision‐making in fields such as security, health‐care, transportation, and environmental monitoring. The growing societal impact and complexity of surveillance necessitate a comprehensive examination of foundational methodologies, key application domains, and the technical, ethical, and operational challenges associated with these systems. Analysis reveals that although AI‐driven surveillance solutions offer improved accuracy, scalability, and responsiveness, they continue to face notable barriers including high computational demands, privacy and data quality concerns, interpretability limitations, and inadequate regulatory frameworks. The review further identifies critical emerging trends, such as sustainable AI practices, human‐AI collaborative models, and the integration of AI with the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain technologies, as significant influences shaping the future trajectory of the field. Addressing these challenges through ongoing research, innovation, and responsible deployment is essential to fully unlock the societal and industrial potential of AI‐enabled surveillance solutions.

documents.abstract: Mobile and application-derived artefacts are becoming more central to digital forensic investigations; however, they can be a diverse set of evidence in a UFDR which are hard to prioritize manually. Mobile and application derived-artifacts are becoming more important to digital forensic investigations, and can be a diverse set of evidence in a UFDR that is difficult to manually prioritize. In the paper, the authors propose an Artificial Intelligence-based UFDR report analysis and intelligent digital forensic investigation assistant to transform the extracted report information into a structured and explainable analysis flow. The prototype now supports reading reports in JSON, XML, CSV and ZIP formats, validates the uploaded report, calculates an integrity checksum (SHA-256), and stores proof of the integrity in SQLite. Twenty behavioral features are created in communication, temporal, browser, application, and file activity. The trained Random Forest (RF) classifier enables three-way classification, and a trained Isolation Forest (Anomaly scoring) is used. A suspicious detector based on the 4 parameters is set, and activates when late-night activity is detected, or when suspicious incoming/outgoing communication, suspicious text indicators or high anomaly scores are detected. The conditions are combined using UNION logic and deduplicated by evidence identifier to return suspicious and/or critical records to the investigators. Risk engine helps transform the model and indicator outputs are mapped to a 0-100 score, and with the help of SHAP Tree Explainer, it is possible to get feature contributions by the model and a human-readable “WHY?” explanation based on evidence. An evidence-based assistant retrieves case, analysis and explanation information from the database and provides a deterministic answer when the language-model service is not available. The accuracy of the test split was 93% and F1-score, recall and macro precision were all approximately 0.93 for the synthetic benchmark that was reproduced using the project. Suspicious-detector tests were also conducted successfully, with special emphasis on specific tests. This system instead of the automatic finding of criminal conduct presents a non-automatic triage system, explainability and a conversational workflow for forensic decision support.

Haul trucks generate more than half of direct greenhouse-gas emissions in typical mining operations, making haulage decarbonization central to the industry’s net zero commitments. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to haulage, but existing reviews examine individual technologies rather than linking them to decarbonization and ESG outcomes. This comprehensive review synthesizes 73 peer-reviewed sources from 2017 to 2026 across route optimization, electric and hybrid trucks, predictive maintenance, fleet monitoring, carbon footprint reduction, and ESG performance, grades reported outcomes by validation basis, and develops a framework linking AI-enabled technology domains, through their operational mechanisms, to ESG outcomes. Reinforcement-learning dispatching reduced haulage emissions by more than 30% relative to fixed scheduling in simulation, trolley assist reduced fuel use by up to 91%, and fleet electrification modeling projected GHG reductions of up to 92.6% in a hypothetical case, contingent on grid carbon intensity. Most reported reductions derive from simulation, and AI’s advantage over conventional control of electrified fleets remains undemonstrated. Gaps include scarce field-verified emission baselines, limited modeling of operator behavior, immature cybersecurity and data governance practice, and weak engagement between ESG research and haulage technology. AI-enabled operational measures offer a promising near-term decarbonization pathway that complements, rather than awaits, fleet electrification.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) raise new questions for instructors, among them how to integrate LLMs productively into coursework and what to evaluate in students' work when an LLM can produce much of it directly. LLM-guided homework assignments offer one answer. Instructors configure the LLM to guide students in ways that achieve specific pedagogical goals, such as recalling material, discovering new concepts, or critically evaluating deliberately flawed reasoning, and grade the full student--LLM conversation, and with it the student's reasoning, rather than only the final answer. In this paper, we report on the large-scale deployment of such assignments, implemented through LLteacher, an open-source tool that supports recall, discovery, and critical-thinking assignments, in a large introductory statistics course serving mostly pre-major undergraduates. Results on 134 students show meaningful gains in self-reported confidence, with over 80\% agreeing that the assignments improved their comprehension of course material and their ability to interpret statistical results; gains were largest among students who started with lower confidence, suggesting this approach may help narrow gaps in preparation. Interaction patterns varied widely, from long single messages to rapid iterative exchanges, and hallucinations, when present, were rarely disruptive to learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.

Patients facing serious illness may experience ambivalence about important treatment decisions, sharing information with loved ones, or, perhaps most consequentially, living in a way that is aligned with their values. Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative, person-centered communication style that explores ambivalence by eliciting a patient's motivations, values, and goals. MI offers a practical framework for serious illness communication (SIC), when patients and families often experience competing priorities and uncertainty. Through a clinical case, this article explores the four fundamental processes of MI-engaging, focusing, evoking, and planning-and reframes these concepts through a SIC lens. We highlight the application and adaptation of micro-skills (open-ended questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summaries) to deepen understanding, explore ambivalence, and support values-concordant decision making. Integrating MI-informed communication strategies into serious illness care provides clinicians with practical tools to navigate ambivalence, foster collaboration, and evoke a patient's intrinsic motivation for decisions aligned with their values.

Abstract Clinical communication is central to patient outcomes, yet large-scale annotation of patient–provider conversations remains labor-intensive, inconsistent, and difficult to scale. Existing large language model (LLM)–based approaches typically rely on single-task systems with limited robustness across communication frameworks and clinical domains. In this study, we developed MOSAIC, a M ulti-framew O rk S tructured Agentic AI system for scalable Clinical C ommunication coding. MOSAIC combines dynamically few-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow for planning, annotation, and verification. Performance was evaluated against gold-standard annotations produced by trained human coders. MOSAIC was developed on 54 annotated transcripts and evaluated on 120 transcripts spanning rheumatology and obstetrics/gynecology (OB/GYN). On the evaluation set, MOSAIC achieved an overall weighted F1 score of 95.6%. Performance was highest in rheumatology (F1 = 95.9%) and strongest for bias and patient behaviors categories (F1 = 96.4% and 96.1%, respectively). These results demonstrate the potential of multi-framework AI systems for reliable clinical communication analysis.

documents.abstract: Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) supports intelligent processing close to where data is generated. However, training machine-learning models across edge devices is difficult when devices have limited memory, processing power, battery capacity, and network bandwidth. Federated learning (FL) addresses one important concern by allowing devices to train a shared model without sending their raw records to a central repository. Nevertheless, model updates may still expose information, while repeated communication and encryption can increase training time and resource use. This paper reviews an integrated architecture that combines federated learning, homomorphic encryption (HE), client clustering, update pruning, adaptive quantization, and convergence-aware stopping. In the architecture, each client trains locally, removes low-impact update values, compresses the remaining update, and encrypts it before transmission. The server aggregates encrypted updates and coordinates the next training round. The source study reports that its FLHC-QPR approach improves accuracy and reduces latency and memory overhead compared with selected comparison methods on a Human Activity Recognition task. The paper explains the architecture, workflow, potential applications, evaluation measures, limitations, and future research directions. The discussion is based on the supplied research article; performance values are reported from that study and are not presented as newly measured results.

Wireless networks and network slicing are undergoing great transformation at sixth generation (6G) ushering in unprecedented flexibility, ultra-low latency and smart provisioning of services in next-generation communication systems. But, the progress has also opened the cyber-attack surface and network slices are increasingly being targeted by increasingly sophisticated and evolving attacks. However, traditional IDSs are incapable of handling complex attacks because of their limited feature extraction ability, poor contextual learning, and lack of model interpretability, which limits their use in security-critical 6G networks. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a new Explainable Deep Learning (XDL) based intelligent intrusion detection system (IDS) for secure 6G network slicing, namely XHCBAN (Explainable Hybrid CNN–BiLSTM–Attention Network). The proposed model combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to model hierarchical spatial features, Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks to capture bidirectional contextual relations, and an Attention Mechanism to focus on the most discriminative security features. Moreover, to obtain transparent and interpretable predictions, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are integrated to measure the effect of individual features on the model's predictions. The proposed framework includes detailed methodology such as Data Processing, Feature Learning, Attention guided Feature refinement, Deep Classification, and Explainability Analysis. Standard metrics such as Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Specificity, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) are used to evaluate model performance and compared to the conventional machine learning and deep learning baselines using SVM, Random Forest, CNN, LSTM, and BiLSTM under a consistent experimental protocol. The proposed XHCBAN framework is believed to provide better intrusion detection accuracy and performance with a strong improvement in model transparency, robustness and reliability. This work introduces a scalable, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)-enabled intrusion detection system for secure AI-powered 6G network slicing, which fosters next-generation intelligent communication infrastructures and paves the way for practical deployment of explainable cybersecurity systems.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

We introduce Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum (AHC), a domain-informed, rule-based training system for Craftax-Full. AHC combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial-state progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded selection, and original-task practice. It uses no LLM inference and keeps all 43 actions available. At 2,005,401,600 PPO rollout transitions, three primary AHC runs obtain native-task return $46.70\pm0.57$ (sample SD), compared with $41.91\pm1.01$ for fresh native PPO-GTrXL with the same student architecture and evaluation protocol. Evaluation uses ten stochastic rollouts on each of 1024 fixed worlds per model. An additional cohort of three AHC runs reaches $46.08\pm1.23$. Two single-component ablations retain similar mean returns, while jointly freezing difficulty and removing inherited progress gives $45.14\pm2.79$. All-67-achievement profiles show that most of the return difference comes from Intermediate achievements, while the deepest-floor achievements remain unsolved. A Skill-Preflight diagnosis with a 14B teacher shows how prerequisite and floor-access constraints restrict practice. AHC and three 14B diagnostic configurations reach aggregate returns near the reported 80B DiCode mean of 45.88 and below the 235B mean of 48.55. These results show that an explicit curriculum without LLM inference can reach returns comparable to those reported for LLM-generated curricula on Craftax-Full, without action masking.

Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.

Asset-backed Islamic financial models rest on risk-sharing (mudarabah, musharakah), genuine ownership of real assets (ijarah, salam, istisna, asset-backed sukuk), and the prohibitions of riba, excessive gharar and maysir. Technology can strengthen these models when it improves traceability of ownership, automates compliant disbursement, widens retail access to fractional claims on real assets, and supports scalable screening and documentation review. This paper examines the application of distributed-ledger technology (blockchain and smart contracts) and large language models (LLMs) to these structures. It surveys use cases, identifies instruments in use or under development globally, and notes constraints of Shariah substance, oracle reliability and human oversight. The paper is a working synthesis for learners and policymakers. It is not a fatwa and does not represent the position of any government or institution. Tokenisation does not by itself confer Shariah compliance; the underlying contract, ownership transfer and risk allocation remain decisive. Monitoring concurrent classroom collaborative reasoning discussions is challenging because instructors have to track collaboration-relevant behaviors across multiple ongoing conversations at once. Existing Human-AI conversational sensemaking systems can scale monitoring upward through summaries and visual abstractions, but these representations may distance users from underlying conversational evidence, e.g., relevant audio and transcript segments, needed to forage downward. Through our formative study, we developed ArguScale, an evidence-grounded Human-AI sensemaking system that organizes interactional signals into temporally aligned representations linked to transcript and audio evidence. A temporal signal-density view provides temporal context and supports rapid cross-group comparison, while selective evidence access allows instructors to inspect audio and transcript. We evaluated ArguScale in a mixed-design study with 20 participants. Compared to other conditions, ArguScale improved participants' ability to efficiently and accurately identify collaboration-relevant cues. We further identify strategies participants used to forage for and make sense of conversational evidence under live time constraints.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has fundamentally disrupted the traditional foundations of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) regimes globally, and more particularly within India. Historically, IPR frameworks have operated on an anthropocentric paradigm, premised entirely on the notion that creative expression and technical innovation flow exclusively from human intellect. This paper presents a doctrinal legal evaluation of the challenges that advanced AI models present to Indian intellectual property architecture, focusing specifically on copyright ownership and patent inventorship. By closely scrutinizing Section 2(d) of the Indian Copyright Act, 1957, alongside Section 2(1)(p) of the Patents Act, 1970, the study highlights the critical statutory gap created by autonomous algorithmic outputs. It further reviews the standard of original human authorship established by the Supreme Court of India in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak, analyzing its compatibility with modern AI training methodologies. The paper evaluates the legal ramifications of utilizing copyrighted datasets without permission, examining the viability of the ‘fair dealing’ exception under Section 52(1)(a). Comparing regulatory strategies across the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union, the paper proposes a sui generis statutory system designed to balance technological promotion with the protection of human creative labor.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Introduction: The digital transformation of healthcare systems has been accompanied, since the early 2020s, by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), further accelerated by the emergence of generative AI and large language models (LLMs). Beyond broad discussions about the potential of AI, healthcare professionals, researchers, and educators need practical guidance regarding available tools, their applications, performance, limitations, and the conditions required for their responsible use. Objective: To provide an international, critical, and educational synthesis of the major applications of AI in clinical practice, biomedical research, and health sciences education, while examining its potential benefits, limitations, associated risks, and the conditions required for safe and responsible use, particularly in resource limited settings. Methods: A structured narrative review of the literature was conducted using publications indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. The literature search was supplemented by institutional documents from the World Health Organization (WHO), UNESCO, and the European Union, as well as selected systematic reviews, evidence syntheses, and regional reports addressing the use of AI in healthcare in sub Saharan Africa. Publications primarily published between 2020 and 2026 were prioritized. Results: Available evidence demonstrates a rapid diversification of AI applications in healthcare. Generative AI systems and LLMs can support medical information synthesis and interpretation, clinical decision support, literature searching, scientific writing and communication, development of educational materials, clinical simulation, and selected epidemiological surveillance activities. These technologies may improve access to information and increase the efficiency of selected healthcare and research tasks. However, their use is associated with important risks, including hallucinations and factual errors, algorithmic bias, potential breaches of data privacy, limited traceability and accountability, and the risk of cognitive dependence among users. These challenges are particularly relevant in healthcare systems with limited human, digital, and regulatory resources. Perspectives: Between 2026 and 2030, advances in multimodal AI, agentic systems, and personalized medicine may substantially expand the scope of AI applications in healthcare. These developments will require robust governance frameworks, scientific validation, human oversight, data protection, and appropriate professional training. Particular attention should be given to the linguistic, cultural, technological, and socioeconomic adaptation of AI solutions to resource limited settings to prevent the widening of existing digital and health inequities. Conclusion: The key challenge is no longer whether AI will be used in healthcare, but how it can be implemented safely, ethically, scientifically, and in alignment with the needs of healthcare professionals and populations. In low and middle income countries, particularly in the Sahel, AI integration should be approached as a gradual process based on rigorous validation, human oversight, capacity building, and context specific governance. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; machine learning; generative artificial intelligence; large language models; clinical decision support; ethics; data privacy; medical education; biomedical research; sub Saharan Africa.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AI is revolutionizing histopathology through its ability to enhance diagnostic precision, efficiency, and uniformity in disease identification and classification. The use of machine learning and deep learning algorithms allows for automated analysis of digital tissue images, which is helpful for cancer detection, tumor grading, classification and prediction of prognosis. AI-driven image processing and feature extraction aid in identifying fine details of morphology and minimize diagnostic variation. But the limitations of data, algorithmic bias, interpretability, data privacy and clinical validation are all important hurdles. The combination of AI, digital pathology, and clinical experience could lead to a more seamless diagnostic process and personalized medicine, aiding in accurate disease diagnosis and positive patient results.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The article presents the results of a survey of 99 teachers of natural science and mathematics disciplines and 195 students in grades 7–11 in Poltava region on the use of AI tools in the educational process. It was found that 96% of teachers and 93.8% of students already use AI, but 64.6% of students did so without any pedagogical guidance. The main systemic barrier for teachers is work overload (66.7%), despite a strong willingness to learn (81.8%). A thematic analysis of students' open-ended responses revealed a dominant message: AI is used primarily to understand material, not to copy it. A critical research gap was identified regarding the specific impact of AI on adolescents as a distinct age group.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

documents.abstract: Retrospective registration of a completed systematic review of studies that developed or evaluated artificial intelligence (AI) or machine learning techniques for the diagnosis, grading, management, or prediction of uveitis in humans. This registration is retrospective; it was submitted after the review was completed (searches, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and synthesis had all been performed).

Nanobodies are compact and stable proteins derived from the variable domain of camelid heavy-chain-only antibodies (VHH). Advances in structural biology, molecular modeling, and artificial intelligence (AI) are shifting VHH discovery from empirical selection toward data-driven design. However, predicted binding alone does not ensure biological activity or successful translation, particularly for antigenically variable pathogens. Complementing recent reviews that broadly survey computational VHH modeling and optimization, this review focuses on how antigen biology and functional epitope prioritization can guide the design of pathogen-targeting VHHs. We organize the field along a structure–function–translation continuum, connecting the structural basis of VHH recognition and available data resources with conventional discovery, antigen-guided de novo design, and sequence–structure learning. We further examine how developability, recombinant production, multispecificity, humanization, structural dynamics, and antigenic variation shape the progression from predicted binders to functional VHHs. Finally, we discuss how multimodal foundation models could integrate these dimensions to support the design of functional, manufacturable, and escape-resilient VHHs.

ABSTRACT Objective This study aims to compare image feature identification and diagnostic performance between artificial intelligence‐aided image‐enhanced endoscopy (using the Storz Professional Image Enhancement System, SPIES) and conventional white‐light endoscopy (WLE) for sinonasal inverted papilloma (SIP). Methods A total of 163 patients were investigated using Storz Professional Image Enhancement System (SPIES) endoscopy (SPIES Spectral A[SA]/Spectral B[SB]) and WLE. From each patient, one or two images (only in the presence of bilateral lesions) were obtained, and a large number of potential features were extracted from WLE, SA, and SB. Independent t‐tests and LASSO methods were used to feature selection. Machine learning (ML) models were trained and evaluated for each channel of images. Results The Random Forest (RF) algorithm on SPIES SB mode achieved superior performance: accuracy = 0.86, sensitivity = 0.89, specificity = 0.83, AUC = 0.86, and Kappa = 0.71. SB significantly outperformed SA (accuracy = 0.77) and WLE (accuracy=0.75). ROC analysis confirmed SB's diagnostic superiority (area under curve [AUC]: SB = 0.86 vs. SA = 0.77, WLE = 0.75). Conclusions SPIES SB mode demonstrated the highest diagnostic accuracy and AUC for SIP identification, highlighting its potential as a superior imaging modality. SPIES endoscopy exhibits superior diagnostic accuracy and predictive performance compared to conventional WLE in the diagnosis of SIP. However, the single‐center design and limited sample size necessitate validation through multicenter studies with larger cohorts.

Two related conceptual research papers by Andreas Ehstand: Articulation Is Not Yet Knowledge, and A Definition Is Not Yet a Mandate. They distinguish changes in expression, meaning and grounds from communicative function, institutional standing and later uptake in human-AI and hybrid systems. Version 0.1 was elaborated on 11 October 2026 with assistance from an AI assistant. Historical internally dated March and April 2026 drafts are research antecedents, not verified earlier publications. This edition reports no empirical study, external peer review, established novelty, standards compliance or performance guarantee. The files contain 24 bilingual working definitions, partly clarifying established expressions, and explicitly constructed civilian counterexamples. This is a conceptual contribution, not a new field glossary. Proprietary procedures, operational instruments, original private materials and business logic are excluded. Existing records are not modified.

While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Authentic assessment has been a recognized aspiration in higher education for nearly four decades, yet its implementation at the undergraduate level has remained constrained by the procedural demands of professional-level work. Generative artificial intelligence reshapes the implementation calculus by lowering the entry barriers that previously confined authentic assessment to capstone courses, professional programs, and elite institutional contexts. This paper presents a single-semester case study of an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course taught to undergraduates in a child and adolescent development program at a regional public university. Twenty-one students used a custom AI class companion without restriction to produce full-length qualitative research manuscripts. The analytic backbone is a five-dimensional model of authentic assessment, with its physical-context dimension extended to require AI inclusion in fields where professional practice now incorporates the technology. Three rubric-proximal proxy indicators were estimated across the corpus: methods specificity, claim-evidence coupling, and theory-interpretation linkage density. The methods specificity proxy compresses toward the upper bound of its scale, indicating that AI scaffolding supports structural elements of qualitative writing effectively. The two judgment-dependent proxies retain wide dispersion. Process tracing of four contrasting cases identifies three pathways that distinguish stronger from weaker outcomes: criteria-based orchestration, irreducible input supply, and substantive iteration. The boundary-condition pattern indicates that authentic assessment in AI-integrated courses remains diagnostic where it needs to be and is supported where it needed support.

Large language models are increasingly used in reflective journaling, where articulating an experience is part of interpreting it. This raises questions about how writers retain authorship, exercise agency, and assess personalized assistance. We present AuthScribe, an LLM-assisted reflective journaling system that combines contextual anchors, writer-steered AI support, Autobiographical Citations, and read-only Provisional Drafts that require re-expression before AI-generated suggestions enter the journal. Retrieval and LLM inference run on-device. In a 14-day field deployment with 14 participants, grounding shifted from situating current experiences to reconnecting them with prior self-authored interpretations. Perceived agency remained stable through Week 1 and shifted during Week 2. Participants described authorship through transforming AI-generated suggestions into personally meaningful expression, and trusted personalized prompts when they could trace them to prior writing. We discuss design implications for adoption friction, longitudinal agency, and traceable personalization in AI systems for personal reflection.

BACKGROUND: Insect pests threaten agricultural productivity, while conventional surveillance is labour-intensive and excessive pesticide use creates environmental and health risks. This review evaluated automated insect detection, counting, classification and monitoring technologies, focusing on machine-learning integration, field transferability, and operational readiness. RESULTS: A PRISMA 2020-guided formal search covering publications from 2010 to 2024 identified 313 records relevant to the technological and methodological scope of the review. After title/abstract screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 116 publications were retained. The evidence encompassed camera- and vision-based systems; acoustic, infrared, and optoelectronic sensors; electrostatic and physical approaches; non-lethal photonic monitoring; radar and biosensing technologies; Internet of Things-enabled platforms; and machine- and deep-learning methods. Camera- and vision-based systems were among the most extensively documented and field-oriented approaches, particularly when integrated with remote image acquisition, communication networks, and automated classification. Acoustic systems provided complementary options for continuous or low-power monitoring, whereas radar, biosensing, and other emerging approaches broadened applications toward biodiversity assessment, large-area surveillance, and early detection. Reported performance was not directly comparable across publications because metrics, acquisition conditions, and validation levels differed substantially, ranging from laboratory or dataset benchmarks to semi-field trials, field validations, and operational deployments. CONCLUSION: No single technology is optimal for all monitoring objectives. Operational adoption requires standardized task-specific reporting, independent and sustained field validation, representative datasets, improved transferability across crops and environments, and system-level assessment of robustness, energy autonomy, connectivity, maintenance, and cost. Sensor fusion, edge artificial intelligence, and domain-adaptive or uncertainty-aware models are promising when they provide measurable decision-support benefits. © 2026 The Author(s). The paper presents an automated system for diagnosing electric locomotive current collectors based on machine vision, which allows for the replacement of time-consuming and subjective manual inspections with non-contact, high-precision measurements. The Python program, using the OpenCV, NumPy, and SciPy libraries, analyzes photos and video streams. It measures the minimum thickness and width of the carbon insert using photos, and tracks the geometric parameters of the current collector in real-time using video with reflective markers, calculating the distances and angles between control points. A 3D model of the current collector has been created for testing purposes. The implementation of the system reduces the influence of the human factor, allows for the detection of defects at an early stage, the prediction of the residual resource of equipment, the reduction of operating costs, and the minimization of the risk of emergencies, thereby increasing the reliability of the power supply for electric rolling stock.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: The increasing deployment of Automated Mobile Vehicles (AMVs) in warehouses requires efficient navigation in dynamic environments shared with human workers. Traditional safety strategies, such as stopping or slowing down, often reduce efficiency and do not account for human-robot interaction. To address this, interaction-aware methods have been developed. However, traditional interaction models assume fixed parameters, rely on a single forecast, or use intent labels that are not updated during the interaction, and thus do not explicitly represent intention uncertainty, that is, variability in how people react to robots. When combined with position uncertainty introduced by sensing noise, this unmodeled intention uncertainty can make motion prediction and navigation decisions unreliable, leading to conservative behavior, inefficiency, or collisions in human–robot interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation (BRAN), a framework that jointly models intention and position uncertainty. BRAN maintains probabilistic beliefs over an agent's position and intention to explicitly represent uncertainty in both quantities. Position uncertainty is represented via sampled observations, and the intent belief is updated online through Bayesian inference so that predictions evolve with the interaction. These beliefs are propagated through the Social Force Model (SFM) to generate predictions of possible agent motion under uncertainty. We then compute collision risk from the predicted motion distribution and incorporate it into model predictive control as a constraint. This constrains predicted collision risk while optimizing motion toward the goal. Experimental results validate the proposed design in controlled settings, demonstrate its effectiveness in scenarios with multiple pedestrians, and confirm its feasibility on a real robot with onboard sensing and actuation.
