Digital work technologies increasingly determine when, how, and at what intensity work is performed. Continuous connectivity, electronic monitoring, algorithmic management, and technology-enabled harassment can generate psychosocial risks that are not adequately addressed by legal rules designed mainly for physical workplaces. This article asks whether Vietnamese labour and occupational safety and health law provides a coherent preventive framework for protecting workers’ mental health in digital work environments and which comparative models can guide reform. It uses doctrinal analysis, interdisciplinary literature synthesis, and functional comparison with international standards and selected approaches in the European Union, France, and Australia. The analysis finds that Vietnamese law contains relevant constitutional, working-time, occupational safety and health, dignity, anti-harassment, and personal-data safeguards, but these rules remain fragmented. In particular, psychosocial risks are not expressly defined or systematically assessed; workers have no statutory right to disconnect; electronic monitoring and algorithmic management are not regulated as working-condition issues; and protection for platform and remote workers remains incomplete. The article proposes an integrated reform model built around seven elements: express recognition of mental health and psychosocial risks; mandatory risk assessment and control; a qualified right to disconnect; transparency, consultation, and human review for digital monitoring and algorithmic decisions; confidential support and return-to-work measures; stronger social dialogue, inspection, and national data; and appropriately extended protection for platform workers. The proposed model treats mental health protection as a preventive labour-law obligation and a condition of sustainable digital transformation rather than as a discretionary employee benefit.

Weak bag-level labels are widely available in computational pathology, whereas reliable instance-level annotations for whole-slide images remain expensive and ambiguous. Weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) achieves strong bag-level classification, but instance-level supervision from attention scores, model predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement may fail to identify class-specific local evidence. We propose ProtoPur, a prototype-purity pseudo-labeling method for weakly supervised instance-level learning in pathology whole-slide images. ProtoPur estimates class-balanced local purity over prototype regions constructed from frozen foundation-model features, and assigns pseudo-labels to high-purity regions strongly associated with a target class. This purity-first design separates class-specific evidence from negative or shared morphology, with coverage used only to ensure sufficient pseudo-label assignment. We provide a PAC-style analysis showing that the risk of an instance classifier trained with ProtoPur pseudo-labels can be decomposed into a standard uniform-convergence term and a ProtoPur-specific pseudo-label noise term, comprising selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual. Experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two pathology foundation encoders show that ProtoPur consistently improves instance-level performance across multiple MIL backbones while maintaining competitive bag-level performance. Pseudo-label quality comparisons on two public datasets further demonstrate that prototype-purity selection provides stronger instance supervision. These results suggest that the foundation-model features contain exploitable instance-level supervision signals, and ProtoPur is a way to reveal and use these signals from weak bag labels without requiring dense instance annotations.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: When people and AI systems produce work together, every result raises the same question: who made what, when, and has it changed since? This conceptual note describes a practice that combines three independently checkable records: a persistent identifier with a registration date, a cryptographic hash of every file, and a blockchain-anchored timestamp. Definitions are published as versions under one concept identifier so that change stays visible. The note states what such records prove and what they do not prove, and shows how the same structure can document human review of AI output: which person checked which result at which time. It is a description of a working practice, not an empirical study.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the ways in which people communicate, perceive language, and process information. Modern AI technologies, including natural language processing, speech recognition, machine translation, and conversational systems, have created new opportunities for studying human speech and psycholinguistic processes. At the same time, these technologies raise important questions about the differences between human language comprehension and machine-based language processing. Human speech is not merely a system of sounds and grammatical structures; it is a complex cognitive and social activity involving memory, attention, emotion, context, and cultural knowledge. This article examines the relationship between human speech, language perception, and psycholinguistic processes in the age of artificial intelligence. It also discusses the potential benefits and limitations of AI in language learning, communication, and linguistic research. The article argues that AI can support human communication and language education, but it cannot fully replace the complex cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions of human language.

Conventional distillation transfers capability through teacher-generated demonstrations. LLM-as-a-Judge knowledge distillation offers a distinct and increasingly practical alternative. In the label-only variant studied here, the student generates every response and improves from scalar scores alone. Prior work shows that this non-demonstrative feedback can improve student capability, but it creates a fundamentally different provenance problem. No teacher-generated answer enters the student's training set, so any evaluator-specific trace must pass through a low-bandwidth reward signal rather than copied text. Existing watermarks and distillation detectors do not cover this score-only channel. We introduce Radioactive Feedback, which encodes a registered pattern of behavioral preferences in the rewards themselves. The evaluator applies bounded pointwise adjustments to quality-qualified responses, allowing repeated optimization to transfer the pattern to a student trained by another party. Experiments on code and mathematics show that the registered preferences transfer through scores alone and across datasets, enabling black-box detection against a fixed reference pool.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

Both primary coupling-versus-uncoupled criteria pass; the full contract fails because dynamic coupling does not outperform matched fixed coupling and the entropy–curvature diagnostic does not exceed its circular-shift surrogate threshold. documents.abstract: Article 2(2)(b) of Turkey’s Law No. 6331 on Occupational Safety and Health excludes the intervention activities of disaster and emergency units from that statute’s scope. The exclusion concerns duties performed during response operations; it does not establish that firefighters lack every protection under other legal or administrative instruments. This evidence-informed legal and policy analysis combines a structured, non-systematic occupational-health evidence synthesis, doctrinal analysis, a review of 43 Turkish judicial decisions issued from 1997 to 2024, and a functional comparison with the United Kingdom. International evidence identifies occupational firefighting as carcinogenic to humans (IARC Group 1), links fire suppression with sharply elevated risk of fatal coronary events, and documents substantial psychological and musculoskeletal burdens. In the official sources examined, no nationally binding firefighter-specific instrument was identified that prescribed post-incident decontamination, detailed health-surveillance content, personal protective equipment performance monitoring, or structured psychological support. The judicial corpus was coded across eight analytical categories; its holdings concentrated on pay, personnel status, compensation, procedure, and jurisdiction rather than concrete preventive OSH duties. We interpret these findings through a structural accountability gap model, under which the statutory exclusion may constrain investigation, data generation, standard-setting, and regulatory learning. The model is interpretive, not a tested causal finding. United Kingdom law provides an illustrative comparator because it retains general employer and enforcement duties without a categorical operational exclusion. The article proposes eight evidence-linked policy options. Their effectiveness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness require prospective evaluation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Introduction: Academic work in higher education increasingly relies on digital tools and Artificial Intelligence (AI). For medical and nursing students, making safe, critical, and responsible use of these technologies is essential to develop self-regulated learning in the face of changing practice scenarios. Objective: To analyze the relationship between the academic use of digital tools and autonomous learning in students of medicine and nursing programs at a higher education institution. Methodology: Quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive-correlational, and cross-sectional study. 80 students were surveyed using a validated instrument. Results: Both variables reported high levels: the academic use of digital tools had an average of 3.71 out of 5, and autonomous learning an average of 3.78. A positive, moderate, and statistically significant association was found between both variables. The ethical and critical use of AI was the technological dimension with the lowest score. Conclusions: There is a favorable relationship between the critical mastery of digital tools and the ability for independent learning. However, institutions should focus their pedagogical efforts on improving information verification, the transparent use of AI, and student self-assessment strategies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis. We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: General-purpose multimodal foundation models are increasingly capable of directly controlling robots, yet improving their manipulation capabilities through autonomous interaction remains challenging. A key challenge to such self-improvement is learning from failures in complex manipulation tasks involving cross-stage dependencies, where an action may succeed locally but cause a later stage to fail. To address this challenge, we introduce ReTrace, a self-improvement framework for robotic manipulation through autonomous physical interaction and retrospective reasoning, without provided demonstrations or model-parameter updates. ReTrace retrospectively traces downstream failures to earlier decisions, proposes targeted corrections, and evaluates them through subsequent interactions. Across attempts, ReTrace progressively consolidates validated corrections into a reusable manipulation skill that guide subsequent execution. We evaluate ReTrace on four real-world manipulation tasks using a Franka Research 3 robot. On the two tasks with strong cross-stage dependencies, GPT-6 Astra-low improves from 0% to 80% success on plug insertion and from 0% to 100% on ball pouring, while GPT-6 Sol-xhigh improves from 0% to 10% and 0% to 90%, respectively. The learned skills also transfer across model and reasoning configurations and reduce inference-time decision cost in most evaluated settings.

This study examines policy–practice gaps in occupational safety and health (OSH) protection among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. A multi-method design combined 14 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with an adapted ILO Vision Zero Fund survey administered to 200 agricultural workers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), and qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Findings showed multidimensional patterns involving occupational protection, working conditions, health-service availability, agricultural practices, and productive autonomy. These patterns coexisted with informal, seasonal, short-term, day-labor, and subsistence work, limited occupational risk coverage, discontinuous prevention and training, and fragmented institutional coordination. Qualitative findings further highlighted women’s combined productive and care roles, local and traditional knowledge, community participation, and heterogeneity across territorial settings and agricultural practices as relevant to prevention and decision-making. Conventional social protection and occupational risk arrangements centered on formal, contributory employment may not fully respond to dispersed and unstable rural work. Strengthening rural OSH requires integrated, territorially adapted, gender-sensitive strategies linking prevention, social protection, sustained training, institutional coordination, community participation, and productive autonomy. The findings support assessing differentiated and progressive protection pathways, including the feasibility of subsidized occupational risk coverage for more vulnerable workers and small productive units, combined with contributory mechanisms where work arrangements are more stable. By linking worker-level realities with institutional and policy-implementation gaps, this study provides evidence to inform more equitable rural OSH policies responsive to diverse territorial realities in Colombia.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Large Language Models accelerate software development but introduce severe security vulnerabilities. This systematic review investigates security risks in automated coding, benchmark limitations, and the role of human developers. Findings indicate that models frequently generate insecure code and faulty patches due to training data biases. Additionally, the models themselves are susceptible to direct attacks. Current evaluation methods suffer from data contamination and lack robust security metrics. Consequently, human oversight remains essential. Safer integration of automation will require more security-aware model architectures, stronger security-specific benchmarks, and more effective human-AI collaboration frameworks to mitigate these systemic risks.

Abstract Based on the theoretical framework of the System Intelligence (SI) Autonomous Governance Protocol (specifically the 13-node structure and resolution equations), this paper defines the Reference Implementation code and execution log format required to perform automated economic redistributions without human intervention. By registering this specification, the technical standards are immutably fixed for autonomous deployment and operation by Layer 4 execution frameworks and AI agent systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used both as recommenders and to explain recommendations, yet producing faithful, user-centric explanations and evaluating them rigorously remain open problems, compounded by a documented reproducibility crisis in recommender systems research. In this work we formalise recommendation as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and propose a unified, three-tier agentic framework that couples a simulation environment (RecoWorld), a reproducible policy engine (RecBole), and a cognitive LLM user agent. As an offline, single-turn validation of this framework on the MovieLens-32M dataset, we benchmark preliminary single-epoch checkpoints of traditional policies (Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), Convolutional Neural Collaborative Filtering and Neural Matrix Factorisation (NeuMF)), generate LLM-based explanations from the BPR recommendations and score them with quantitative diversity, faithfulness, counterfactual and readability metrics over roughly one million user-item pairs, and run an LLM-as-user interview simulation in which explanations produced by a Qwen2.5 explainer are assessed by a Llama-3 respondent through a six-criterion explanation-quality survey; a controlled comparison on 2000 users shows that replacing BPR with the more accurate NeuMF policy leaves these survey scores practically unchanged. The generated explanations prove highly faithful (feature precision 0.9996, sufficiency 0.9999) and user-tailored explanations (unique-sentence ratio 0.9978), and simulated users rate clarity highest (3.86/5) yet trust lowest (2.60/5). Faithful template explanations are, therefore, trusted less than they are understood, motivating a shift towards controllable generative explanation and scalable simulated evaluation.

Designing a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detector that is tailored to each specific deployment site can improve detection performance, yet most existing detectors, including deep-unfolding methods, adapt mainly within human-prescribed algorithmic structures. This letter proposes SiteEvo, a site-adaptive agentic discovery framework that extends adaptation from parameter tuning to detector-algorithm discovery. Rather than selecting or recombining predefined architectures, the large language model (LLM) agent synthesizes complete executable detector programs under a common design contract by combining its pretrained communication knowledge, site-specific wireless evidence, and experience accumulated during the search. Each proposal defines its own processing structure and trainable parameterization, and the parameters are optimized by a communication-system backend. The resulting high-performance detector is further structurally refined to reduce block-level computational cost under a bit error rate (BER)-preservation constraint and is finally frozen for deployment without online LLM inference. Simulations across three sites demonstrate BER reductions by factors of 2.6 to 6.0 over the best-performing competing detector at each site at 6 dB, while structural refinement reduces block-level computational cost by 16.7-34.1% under a validation-BER constraint.

This conceptual design article proposes situated AI judgement as a teaching and assessment model for responsible generative AI use in higher education. It argues that students need to learn not only how to use AI tools, but also how to evaluate, challenge, revise, and refuse AI outputs in relation to disciplinary standards, evidence, and ethical boundaries. Building on evaluative judgement and assessment scholarship, the article presents a four-stage model: pre-AI interpretation, structured AI dialogue, critical comparison, and reflective accountability. The model is developed through an anthropology and heritage studies activity in which students analyse public nomination files submitted under UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, especially the nomination of Momoeria, New Year’s celebration in eight villages of Kozani area, West Macedonia, Greece. The article shows how this case can help students examine institutional language, community participation, safeguarding, consent, visibility, and decontextualisation while judging the limits of AI-generated summaries. It contributes to applied learning and teaching by offering an assessment design that makes AI-mediated judgement visible and may be adaptable across disciplinary contexts, with a brief inclusive education example illustrating how the same logic might be adapted beyond heritage studies. The article operationalises responsible AI use not as disclosure or compliance alone, but as an assessable capacity to interpret, verify, critique, and ethically limit AI use within a specific field.

documents.abstract: Audio-Visual Segmentation (AVS) requires predicting pixel-wise masks of sounding objects by grounding acoustic signals in visual space. In multi-source scenes, concurrent sound sources often remain entangled within shared visual representations, leading to merged masks or unstable specialization when using standard alignment-focused transformer architectures. To address this, we present SlotAVS, an object-centric framework driven by competitive bi-modal slot attention. While robust foundation models provide rich semantic priors, SlotAVS shifts the paradigm from global cross-modal fusion to explicit competitive binding. By initializing discrete object slots from temporal audio sequences and enforcing strict slot-wise competition over spatial visual tokens, our method structurally mitigates the blending of distinct acoustic entities. Further, to stabilize instance-level learning, we introduce a Hungarian matching strategy that optimally aligns slots with ground-truth objects using spatial and boundary overlap. Coupled with a numerically stable, confidence-aware mask fusion mechanism, SlotAVS robustly aggregates multi-source predictions. Extensive experiments on the AVSBench dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving 88.6% mIoU on the Single-Source (S4) split and 71.7% mIoU on the Multi-Source (MS3) split. These results show that explicit competitive binding is critical for complex audio-visual scene understanding and effectively leveraging foundation-model priors without relying solely on their capacity.

The increasing complexity of modern power distribution networks and the integration of renewable energy sources require intelligent and reliable fault management systems. This paper presents , a smart grid framework that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and edge computing for real-time fault detection, prediction, and restoration. The proposed system continuously monitors electrical parameters such as voltage, current, and power using sensors. Edge-based processing enables rapid identification of abnormal conditions and facilitates automated fault isolation and power rerouting through relay-based switching. Machine learning techniques are incorporated to analyze historical and real-time data for fault classification and predictive maintenance. A NodeMCU (ESP8266) module enables remote monitoring and real-time fault notifications through Telegram, while an LCD provides local visualization of grid parameters and system status. The proposed approach aims to reduce fault detection time, minimize power interruptions, improve maintenance efficiency, and enhance the reliability and resilience of smart grid networks

UAV-based vehicle detection has important application value in the fields of intelligent transportation, urban security and emergency rescue. It is the key technology for realizing high-altitude situational awareness and dynamic monitoring. However, in this scenario, the vehicle targets generally have the problems of being small in size, densely distributed, and mutually occluded, which leads to the model being prone to feature loss, missed detections, and high false detection rates. To address these challenges, we propose a vehicle small-target and occluded-target detection method called the small object and occlusion detection method (SOD-YOLO), which is based on YOLOv13. This method includes three main innovations. First, we designed a sliding-window self-attention convolutional structure, a small object and occlusion detection convolution structure (SOD-C2f), which is based on the existing sliding-window self-attention (SWSA) structure. It is suitable for extracting features of small vehicle targets. Through the self-attention mechanism within the local window, we enhance the fine-grained expression of small target features, effectively improving the model’s perception and positioning ability for tiny vehicle targets. Afterward, we integrate the coordinate attention mechanism (CA) by explicitly modeling the interchannel dependencies and spatial position information to achieve precise semantic alignment of features at different levels, significantly enhancing the detection robustness in occluded scenarios. Finally, we employ the Space-to-Depth Convolution (SPDConv) module, which splits the spatial dimension and replaces the traditional stride convolution and pooling layer with nonstride convolution. This approach avoids the loss of fine-grained features during downsampling and further retains the key spatial information of small vehicle targets. The experimental results show that the precision, recall, average mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 of the proposed SOD-YOLO algorithm are 77%, 74.8%, 80.9% and 54.9%, respectively. Compared with the benchmark model YOLOv13, the three indicators increase by 3.6%, 1.1%, 3.6% and 2.6%, respectively. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm performs better in the tasks of detecting small targets and occluded vehicles and is able to better meet the precise detection requirements of vehicle targets from a high-altitude perspective.

Long-running conversational AI agents and assistive development models inevitably succumb to contextual degradation, specification drift, and sycophantic decay. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms treat dialogue turns, human identity, and technical parameters as an undifferentiated, flat vector repository. This structural limitation induces lossy compression of technical truth, context window pollution, and hallucinatory synthesis of project constraints. This paper introduces the architecture of Blue Synergy CORTEX, an external, persistent cognitive runtime operating via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and stateful REST gateways. CORTEX establishes an architectural Tri-Stream Memory Boundary, bifurcating context into three distinct operational lifecycles: an evolving User Stream (Cognitive Blueprint), an audited Identity Stream (Executive Calibration with immutable Core Axioms), and an invariant, non-decaying Knowledge Stream (Living Canonical Specifications). To permanently eliminate specification drift, the Knowledge Stream utilizes a Dual-Zone Ingestion Pattern that couples sub-20ms fast-append staging buffers with scheduled, non-destructive canonical refactoring governed by an algorithmic Semantic Invariant Guard. Operational telemetry is protected by a Cognitive Immunity Shield, ensuring runtime tool crashes and apologetic model artifacts are filtered from long-term memory. Context retrieval executes via a deterministic, zero-LLM topological pathway achieving sub-65ms latency. Finally, we formalize the compliance model under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689, Articles 5, 14, and 15), backed by quantitative benchmark metrics demonstrating 98% factual faithfulness and a 2% hallucination rate.

AI systems can support national-security analysis, but task capability does not establish legitimate decision authority or the superiority of a particular institutional design. This paper proposes a federated governance framework separating evidence ownership, analytical services, decision assurance, human authorization and accountability. A nine-layer role map and staged maturity scenarios organize proposed responsibilities and failure questions. Artificial superintelligence is treated as a hypothetical contingency, not an established or imminent capability. A useful result would require a bounded prospective comparison showing improved analytical quality or correction behavior without unacceptable burdens, disclosure, rights or accountability failures. No implemented national system, empirical finding of superiority, operational deployment or specialist endorsement is reported. Institutional feasibility and distributional effects remain unestablished and require independent policy, legal, security and human-factors review. documents.abstract: Thermodynamic computing lets stochastic physical dynamics carry out a computation and reads out the result as a time average. Recently, thermodynamic computing has been demonstrated on several hardware platforms, including digital CMOS circuits based on stochastic computing. Superconducting single-flux-quantum (SFQ) logic offers very high clock rates and very low switching energy, but it heavily penalizes state, memory, fan-out, and feedback, i.e., exactly the per-neuron accumulators on which such designs rely. We therefore realize thermodynamic computing in SFQ logic through a co-design of a generative model and its circuit in which the datapath holds no state at all. The model is a class-conditional flow-matching image generator, which transforms Gaussian noise into an image of the requested class along a short, deterministic path of four Euler steps; in hardware, these steps are unrolled into a feed-forward pipeline of stochastic bitstream operators, whose output is read out as a time average, as in thermodynamic computing, without any relaxation phase. Each layer of the model is a butterfly-factorized linear map built exclusively from multiplexers that operate on split-unipolar bitstreams. The ReLU activation, which in stochastic computing requires a per-neuron up/down counter (accounting for 60-70% of the JJs in a counter-based design), is replaced by a stateless AND-NOT gate whose one-clock input skew is provided at no cost by SFQ gate-level pipelining. The models are trained directly on the stream representation of the hardware, with a regularizer that bounds the stream gains. Synthesis with an SFQ design flow shows that stochastic streams tolerate relaxed path balancing, which reduces the Josephson-junction (JJ) count of a hard-wired stage by 40-47%.

Existing navigation systems commonly rely on dedicated depth sensors or explicit depth reconstruction, while learning to generate trajectories directly from RGB images remains challenging due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this work, we propose Stereo-Planner, an end-to-end vision-to-trajectory framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real planning from stereo RGB observations. The key idea is to formulate trajectory generation as state- and scale-conditioned querying of latent stereo geometry. A Scene Representor incorporates a pretrained vision grounding foundation model to extract geometric cues shared across simulated and real-world environments, supporting generalization across visual domains. A lightweight Trajectory Decoder then translates these representations into trajectories through interleaved attention, separating trajectory-state interaction from scene-feature retrieval and incorporating the stereo baseline as a metric-scale cue. With these designs, Stereo-Planner is trained entirely on simulated data by minimizing differentiable trajectory costs and deployed directly in real-world environments without fine-tuning. Benchmark results demonstrate strong cross-scene generalization, with a 95% success rate in simulation environments at a commanded speed of 8 m/s, and competitive performance against depth-based planners using only stereo RGB observations for scene perception. Furthermore, deployment on a compact quadrotor equipped with an NVIDIA Orin NX enables autonomous flight at speeds of up to 7 m/s, with a mean onboard vision-to-action inference time of 24.27 ms. The software, simulation environments, and hardware designs will be open-sourced at https://github.com/Stereo-Planner/Stereo-Planner.

This study aims to identify artificial intelligence (AI) application areas and develop a strategic technology roadmap in the tourism and hospitality industry. The study employs structural topic modeling approach and analyzes patent data from 2010 to 2024. A total of 866 patents (2010–2019) and 3,822 patents (2020–2024) are analyzed to identify application areas. During 2010–2019, applications focused on guest experience, personalization, and efficiency. During 2020–2024, the emphasis shifted towards health, safety, and personalized wellness. Further, the strategic roadmap for AI technology was prepared for near-term (0–2 years), mid-term (2–5 years), and long-term (5–10 years). By leveraging patent data as codified knowledge of innovation, the study contributes to the field of knowledge management by mapping how technological capabilities evolve and become embedded in organizational processes. Overall, the study offers valuable insights into the changing landscape of AI applications and their implications for the tourism and hospitality industry.

Long-term memory for assistants needs a gate that decides when a new utterance retires an old stored claim. Benchmark labels for this step mark a pair as changed or not, so they cannot tell a gate that acts on established change from one that acts on a hint. We write a task contract that separates the two (SUPERSEDED vs. NEEDS-CONFIRMATION vs. COMPATIBLE), label 500 test pairs built from STALE (change pairs plus same-user controls) with three LLM annotators and two human adjudicators (one author and a second annotator; provenance reported), and evaluate Jev, a typed "System One" decision model, under pre-registered hypotheses. Of the 179 test pairs STALE marks as changed, 72 meet the contract's bar for an established change. Jev never retired a claim on 141 same-conversation non-changes. Its failure is premature retirement: the binary gate retires 39.2% of claims whose change is only suggested. A three-way decision cuts this to 15.5% at a 15.3-point detection cost, which misses our pre-registered 10-point budget, and it lands on the binary gate's own threshold frontier; these verdicts hold under three readings of the gold labels. On a held-out vault scored against a second annotator's labels, a cascade that escalated uncertain cases to a reasoning model and looked best on development data was indistinguishable from simply raising the threshold (premature retirement 26.8% vs. 6.5% on dev). Part of the gap comes from the gold labels: relative to that annotator's reading, LLM-majority gold shares most of its errors with a same-family escalation model, and an identity for binary labels says how much such shared errors hide. The rest is small-sample selection on development data. For builders this means a binary score should not be wired to delete: route suggested changes to pending evidence, and do not trust a cascade selected on development data of this size.

Enabling the reuse and composition of knowledge and capabilities distributed across foundation models is an important step toward building scalable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. However, architectural differences and incompatible representations make it difficult to transfer and integrate these capabilities through a unified cross-model interface. To address this challenge, we propose SuperAI, a cross-architecture multi-model fusion framework that integrates complementary capabilities from multiple source models into a host model through orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations. Specifically, we first extract task-relevant representations from the source models and the host model using shared anchor samples, and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to construct low-dimensional functional subspaces with the same dimensionality. Next, we use orthogonal Procrustes mappings to align the source and host coordinate systems, establishing cross-model correspondences while preserving the internal geometry of each source subspace. Finally, we train a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) with joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments, learning input-dependent residual increments that are injected into the host model for multi-model capability fusion. Experiments on three host models across 15 capability domains show that SuperAI achieves higher average domain scores than the evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods and better preserves general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.
